text: We've built subscriptions, and we've picked delivery extensions. The last piece is telling a subscription when to actually run — and Reporting Services gives you two genuinely different ways to do that.

A shared schedule is created once, as its own item, and then referenced by any number of reports and subscriptions. A report-specific schedule is defined inline, right inside the one subscription that uses it — no separate item to manage. Both express the same recurrence patterns — hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or a one-time run. The difference is entirely about where that information lives, and how many things can point at it. If ten subscriptions all need to run at 6 AM after a nightly load finishes, a shared schedule means "6 AM" lives in exactly one place — move the load to 6:30, and you edit one schedule instead of ten. Shared schedules can also be paused and resumed, which a report-specific schedule simply can't do. Delete a shared schedule that's in use, though, and Reporting Services doesn't orphan anything — it creates an individual report-specific schedule for every subscription that used it, copying the same timing over first, so nothing silently stops running.

None of this runs itself — it's backed by real infrastructure. Creating a schedule writes its recurrence information to the report server database and creates a SQL Server Agent job. When that job fires, it drops an event into a queue the Scheduling and Delivery Processor polls — every 10 seconds, by default. The processor picks the event up, calls the report processor to run the report, and hands the result to whichever delivery extension the subscription specifies. Stop SQL Server Agent for a stretch of time, and every scheduled operation that should have fired during that window is simply lost — it isn't queued up to catch up later.
That's Chapter 7 — subscriptions built, delivery extensions chosen, schedules understood. Next up, Chapter 8: Deployment and Administration, starting with Report Server administration itself.
